analysis.one_liner: Reinstates a tax on oil producers' windfall profits to fund heating aid and home weatherization for low-income households.
analysis.headline: Introduced during the 1990 Gulf crisis oil price spike, the bill never got a committee vote and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: After Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, oil prices jumped and domestic oil producers earned large profits above their normal costs. This bill would bring back the windfall profit tax on domestic crude oil, which had been repealed in 1988, setting the taxable threshold at the average price before the crisis. Half the money raised would go into a dedicated fund for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance program and for weatherizing poor households' homes, paid out automatically each quarter without needing a new vote of Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households that struggle to pay heating bills, who would receive additional LIHEAP heating assistance and free home weatherization funded by a dedicated share of the oil tax; federal deficit reduction would get the other half of the revenue.

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the windfall profit tax on domestic crude oil, which was repealed by the Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988, and repeals the phaseout so the tax becomes permanent.

Sets the base price at the average price per barrel over the four months ending July 31, 1990 — before the Gulf crisis price run-up — so the tax falls only on profits from the sudden spike, not on normal returns.

Creates a Low Income Energy Support Trust Fund and transfers 50 percent of the windfall tax revenue to it, earmarking 7/8 for LIHEAP heating grants and 1/8 for the home weatherization program, paid out quarterly without further appropriation.

Requires the trust fund money to supplement, not replace, existing energy assistance funding, and keeps it flowing only as long as Congress directly appropriates at least $1.5 billion a year for LIHEAP and $200 million for weatherization.

Tightens the tax by treating crude oil futures contracts as taxable crude oil, limiting the 'newly discovered oil' exemption to oil from newly drilled wells, and requiring first-in, first-out inventory accounting so oil inventory holders cannot defer taxes through last-in, first-out accounting during rising prices.

analysis.who_pays: Domestic crude oil producers pay the excise tax on profits above the pre-crisis base price, and futures sellers on crude oil face the tax as well; some of the cost could surface at the pump if producers raise prices.

drawbacks.text: The original windfall profit tax of 1980 was criticized for discouraging domestic oil production and increasing reliance on imports; a good-faith opponent would argue this version could likewise reduce domestic drilling, since oil from previously proven properties would not qualify for the newly discovered oil exemption.

An excise tax on producers is not guaranteed to stay with producers; some of it could be passed through to consumers in higher gasoline and heating oil prices, working against the households the bill aims to help.

The aid mechanism depends on Congress continuing large direct appropriations — at least $1.5 billion a year for LIHEAP — before any trust fund money can flow, so the guarantee is only as durable as future appropriations decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would capture a narrow slice of the profits oil producers earned from a war-driven price spike and route it directly to households hit hardest by heating costs, with automatic quarterly funding that avoids annual budget fights. The honest tradeoffs: it could modestly discourage domestic production and raise import dependence, some of the tax could reach consumers at the pump, and the aid guarantee hinges on Congress maintaining direct appropriations. On balance the design is simple and targeted, but the production-discouragement objection that accompanied the original 1980 tax would apply here too.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then to two subcommittees, but no committee ever voted on it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Donnelly introduced the bill on September 30, 1990, during the oil price spike that followed Iraq's invasion of Kuwait.
It was referred jointly to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and Labor committees on the day of introduction.
In October 1990 it was referred to the Energy and Power subcommittee and the Human Resources subcommittee, and no further action was taken in the remaining months of the Congress.
The bill had six Democratic cosponsors and no recorded vote of any kind before the Congress ended in January 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Domestic oil producers came out ahead: they kept the full profits from the 1990 Gulf crisis price spike and paid no windfall tax, while low-income households never received the dedicated heating-assistance and weatherization funding the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil producers and no one else

for.name: Rep. Brian Donnelly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 30, 1990 and assembled the Low Income Energy Support Trust Fund design.

for.name: 6 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Brennan, McCloskey, and Hertel, who joined as original cosponsors.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after referral; no markup or vote was held before the Congress ended.

against.name: Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Energy and Power subcommittee on October 15, 1990; no action followed.

against.name: Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Human Resources subcommittee on October 26, 1990; no action followed.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats among 257 House Democrats, and no Republican is recorded as supporting or opposing the bill before it died in committee.

industries.note: The bill would tax their profits above the pre-crisis base price permanently, capturing roughly the windfall from the 1990 Gulf crisis price spike. Half the revenue would go to heating aid for poor households, so the industry's gain in keeping the profits is the public's lost benefit.

industries.industry: Oil inventory holders and refiners using LIFO accounting
industries.note: The bill bans last-in, first-out accounting for crude oil inventories and requires first-in, first-out, eliminating a tax deferral that becomes especially valuable when prices are rising.
The bill makes futures contracts on crude oil taxable under the windfall profit tax, closing a channel that would otherwise let sellers capture spike profits outside the tax.

industries.industry: Low-income energy assistance providers (LIHEAP grantees and weatherization agencies)
industries.note: The bill creates a dedicated, automatically funded stream for LIHEAP grants and home weatherization, on top of required direct appropriations, giving these programs a more reliable revenue base.
